orderRules: The tasks can go in any order and on any days (§7). Two can be combined in one outing.

sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline asks for daily movement, fundamental motor skills, games, and swimming where available, and adds for Grades 3–5 basic fitness benchmarks and team sport fundamentals (§3I). Physical Education sits in the weekly queue and is tracked as weekly minutes, not as a daily lesson (§7).

At this age the aim is a child who moves well and enjoys it: who can run, throw, catch, kick, jump and balance with confidence, knows the basics of a few team games, and spends real time outdoors. Restful learning (§1, scholé) applies here too. Unhurried time outside is part of the curriculum, not a break from it.

blocks.text: The tasks can go in any order and on any days (§7). Two can be combined in one outing.
36 weeks in 6 six-week terms, following the seasons (a school year starting in late summer or early autumn is assumed; shift the terms to suit your climate).
4 tasks a week, so 24 per term.
Weekly target: about 150 minutes of the four tasks together, logged as actual minutes.
Beyond the four tasks, children need plenty of free active play every day. Common health guidance for children is an hour of activity a day; the tasks are part of that, not all of it.

blocks.text: Team sport fundamentals (soccer, basketball, softball) are taught as skills and small-sided games, two or three a side. Full matches with rules and positions belong to later grades or a local league.
Colonial games link to History: children in the 1700s played hoop and stick, tug-of-war, marbles, nine-pins and graces (tossing a hoop between two sticks).
Swimming is listed "where available" (§3I). Families with access to a pool, lake or lessons can swap it into task D in any term; Term 6 makes it the focus.

Grades 3–5 add basic fitness benchmarks (§3I). They're measured three times a year: week 1, week 18 and week 36. They're personal bests, not grades: the child competes only with their own earlier numbers.

head: Benchmark
What's measured
A good Grade 3 goal
rows: Push-ups with good form (knees down is fine at first); curl-ups in one minute
A shuttle run between two lines, timed
Jump-rope jumps in a row; catches in a row with a partner

blocks.text: Arithmetic link: measuring the sit-and-reach in inches and timing the shuttle run use Arithmetic's Term 2 measurement and time lessons.
Warm up (five minutes of easy movement) before every task C and every game.
Water, sun and weather: a water bottle every time; hats and sunscreen in summer; layers in winter.
Swimming: always with an adult watching who can swim, and in lessons or a supervised place where possible.
Tumbling on a mat or soft grass, never on a hard floor.
A child who is unwell or hurt rests. Minutes can be made up later or not at all.
Physical Education isn't graded.
Weekly minutes log: actual minutes for each task, which also serves states that require hour-logging (§9).
Benchmarks three times a year (§4), recorded as personal bests.
Skills checklist each term: can the child do the term's skills with confidence? Yes, or not yet.
Sportsmanship is part of every game: taking turns, following rules, winning and losing graciously. Note it; don't score it.

head: Course
Link
rows: The Virginia reel (Term 3) is a dance of the Colonial period
Outdoor walks feed the nature journal

Fortitude in a cold-morning hike, temperance in effort and rest, justice in how a team treats its weakest member (§3J). Each term's virtue follows the year's order (Faith and Hope, Temperance, Fortitude, Justice, Prudence, Charity)
Groundskeeping and heavy work (the Workshop track), and the Outdoor Skills Program elective, are separate but add to the child's active time

blocks.text: Minutes carry over, but don't double up. A missed week is simply a missed week (§9: recovery mode, not overdue badges).
Bad weather: swap task D for an indoor game, dancing or a walk in a covered place.
A skill that isn't coming gets another week; the term's games still go on.

Balls (playground, soccer, basketball, softball and glove), a jump rope, a frisbee, cones or markers, a mat or soft area for tumbling, a stopwatch or phone timer, a tape measure, a hoop and stick, marbles, and a long rope for tug-of-war. Swimming gear where available. Each term manual lists anything special.

sections.title: 10. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: For each week: the skill lesson with its teaching points, the game with simple rules, the fitness work, and an outdoor suggestion. For each term: the colonial game, a skills checklist and a minutes log. In weeks 1, 18 and 36: the benchmark sheet.

terms.title: Early Autumn · Running, Throwing and Catching

head: Skills
Running form · starting, stopping and changing direction · overhand throw · catching · dodging
rows: Freeze tag · sharks and minnows · target toss · catch relays · steal the bacon · colonial game: hoop and stick
Benchmarks in week 1 · building a steady jog · first push-ups and curl-ups
Nature walks, with the nature journal
A skill · B game · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Every time: five minutes of warm-up first (easy jogging, arm circles, leg swings), and water on hand.

blocks.text: Running form. Arms bent and swinging forward and back (not across the body); lean a little forward; land on the front of the foot; eyes ahead. Run short stretches slowly with good form, then faster.
Freeze tag. One child is "it". Anyone tagged freezes until another player crawls through their legs.
Benchmark day. Measure and record each benchmark on the sheet below.
A nature walk. Find something for the nature journal.
Starting, stopping, changing direction. Set out cones or shoes in a zigzag. Run to each, stop with feet apart and knees bent, turn, and go. Then "go" and "stop" on a whistle.
Sharks and minnows. The minnows run from one side to the other; the shark tags them. Tagged minnows become sharks.
Jog without stopping for 5 minutes. Then stretch: reach for the toes, hold for ten seconds, and don't bounce.
A walk, a bike ride or outdoor play.
The overhand throw. Stand side-on to the target. Arm back, step toward the target with the opposite foot, throw, and follow through across the body. Practice with a small soft ball or beanbag.
Target toss. Throw at a target (a hoop on the ground, a chalk circle on a wall) from three distances. Score 1, 2 or 3 points. (Adding scores is Arithmetic practice.)
Jog 6 minutes. Push-ups: learn good form, with a straight back from head to knees (knees down) or to feet. Do as many good ones as you can.
A short hike.
Catching. Hands ready in front. For a high ball, thumbs together; for a low ball, little fingers together. Watch the ball all the way into the hands, and pull it in with "soft hands".
Catch relay. Teams pass a ball down the line by throwing and catching; a drop sends it back to the start.
Jog 7 minutes. Curl-ups: knees bent, feet flat, arms crossed; curl up until the shoulder blades lift. Count how many in one minute.
A nature walk.
Dodging. Fake one way, go the other; stay low and light on the feet. Practice dodging a partner who tries to tag you in a small square.

Colonial game: hoop and stick. Roll a hoop (a hula hoop or a large ring) and keep it rolling by tapping it with a stick. Children in the 1700s raced their hoops down the street. Race to a line and back.
Jog 8 minutes. Push-ups and curl-ups.
A longer walk or hike.
Skills checklist (below): show each of the term's skills.
Steal the bacon. Two teams, each player with a number; a "bacon" (a beanbag) in the middle. When a number is called, those two players race to grab the bacon and get back without being tagged.
Jog as long as you can, up to 10 minutes, and record the time.
A family walk or outing.
Personal bests. The child competes only with their own later numbers (weeks 18 and 36).

head: Benchmark
How to measure
Week 1
rows: Minutes of jogging without stopping (stop at 10)
Sit with legs straight, feet against a box; reach forward slowly along a ruler; measure in inches
Run to a line 10 yards away and back, twice; time it
Jumps in a row without a miss
Catches in a row with a partner, about 10 feet apart

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: Runs with good form (arms forward and back, eyes ahead)
Starts, stops and changes direction under control
Throws overhand, stepping with the opposite foot
Catches a soft ball with "soft hands"

blocks.text: Fun first. At this age a child who enjoys moving will keep moving. Keep the lessons short and the games long.
Good form before speed. Correct one thing at a time, gently.
Siblings and friends make every game better. Most of these games work with two to ten children.
Virtue this term: Faith and Hope. PE's part is small: keep trying the throw that won't come yet, in hope that it will.

Small soft balls or beanbags · a playground ball · cones or markers · a hoop and stick · a stopwatch or phone timer · a ruler or tape measure and a box (for sit-and-reach) · a jump rope · water bottles

terms.title: Late Autumn · Kicking, Soccer and Balance

head: Skills
Kicking · dribbling with the feet · passing and receiving · balance · shooting on goal
rows: Kickball · red light, green light dribbling · small-sided soccer (2 against 2, 3 against 3) · colonial game: tug-of-war
Building toward a 10-minute jog · sit-and-reach practice · push-ups and curl-ups
Autumn hikes · raking and hauling leaves
A skill · B game · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Every time: warm up for five minutes, and have water on hand. Shin guards are a good idea for soccer.

blocks.text: Kicking. Put the non-kicking foot beside the ball, pointing at the target. For a pass, kick with the inside of the foot; for distance, with the laces (top of the foot). Follow through toward the target.
Kickball. Like baseball, but the pitcher rolls a playground ball and the batter kicks it.
Jog 8 minutes. Sit-and-reach: practice reaching slowly, holding at the farthest point for a count of three.
A hike in autumn colors.
Dribbling with the feet. Small touches with the inside and outside of the foot, keeping the ball close; look up between touches.
Red light, green light dribble. On "green", dribble forward; on "red", stop the ball under your foot. Anyone whose ball rolls away goes back to the start.
Jog 8 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
Rake leaves and haul them in a wheelbarrow or tarp. It's real work and good exercise. (The Workshop track's groundskeeping does the same.)
Passing and receiving. Pass with the inside of the foot to a partner; receive by stopping the ball with the inside of the foot or the sole, then pass back. Count passes in a row.
Two against two soccer with small goals (two shoes or cones for each), no goalkeepers.
Jog 9 minutes.
A walk or bike ride.
Balance. Stand on one foot for 10, then 20 seconds; then with eyes closed. Walk heel-to-toe along a line, a low curb or a board on the ground.
Colonial game: tug-of-war. Two teams on a long rope with a marker in the middle; pull the other team across a line. (History reads about colonial life this term.)
Jog 9 minutes; sit-and-reach practice.
A hike.
Shooting on goal. Dribble, then kick with the laces toward a corner of the goal, keeping the ball low.
Three against three soccer with small goals.
Jog 10 minutes, if you can. Push-ups and curl-ups.
A walk or outdoor play.
Skills checklist (below).
A soccer game, or kickball, with family and friends.
Jog as long as you can, up to 10 minutes, and record it.
A family outing.

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: Kicks with the inside of the foot and with the laces
Dribbles with small touches, keeping the ball close
Passes to a partner and stops a pass
Balances on one foot for 20 seconds

blocks.text: Small games teach more. In 2 against 2, every child touches the ball constantly. Large-team games leave most children standing.
Raking counts. Real outdoor work is good exercise, and children are proud of it.
Virtue this term: Temperance. Taking turns, not hogging the ball, and stopping to rest before getting worn out are all temperance on the field.
A size 3 or 4 soccer ball · cones or shoes for goals · a playground ball for kickball · a long rope for tug-of-war · a rake and wheelbarrow or tarp · shin guards (optional) · water bottles

terms.title: Winter · Jump Rope, Tumbling and the Virginia Reel

head: Skills
Jumping rope · forward roll · log roll and balances · cartwheel · jump-rope tricks
rows: Indoor obstacle courses · Simon says · the Virginia reel, a colonial folk dance · colonial game: marbles
Benchmarks in week 18 (the midyear check) · indoor fitness on cold days
A skill · B game or dance · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Winter weather. Many of this term's tasks work indoors. Clear a space, and use a mat, a folded blanket or a soft carpet for tumbling. Never tumble on a hard floor.
Fine Arts link. The Virginia reel was danced in the colonies and the early republic. Fiddle music for it is easy to find. Fine Arts is singing "Yankee Doodle" this term, which works for dancing too.

blocks.text: Jump rope. Turn the rope with the wrists, not the whole arm; jump just high enough to clear it, landing softly on the front of the feet. Start with one jump per turn.
Indoor obstacle course: crawl under a table, step through hoops, balance along a line of tape, toss a beanbag into a basket. Time it, then beat your time.
Indoor fitness: jumping jacks, a minute of jump rope, push-ups and curl-ups.
Snow play or a winter walk, dressed warmly in layers.
The forward roll (on a mat). Squat, hands flat on the mat, tuck the chin to the chest, push with the feet, and roll on the back of the shoulders, never the head. Come up to a squat.

The Virginia reel, part 1. Two lines facing each other, partners opposite. Everyone steps forward and bows (or curtsies) and steps back; then forward, take your partner's right hand, turn once around, and back to place.
Indoor fitness circuit; jump rope for as many jumps in a row as you can.
Sledding or a winter hike.

Log roll and balances. Lie straight, arms overhead, and roll like a log across the mat. Then balances: on one foot with arms out (an "airplane"), and on one knee and the opposite hand. Hold each for five seconds.
The Virginia reel, part 2. Add the left-hand turn, the two-hand turn, and the do-si-do: partners pass right shoulders, go back to back, and return passing left shoulders.
Jog or jump rope 10 minutes, mixed, indoors or out.
A winter walk. Look for animal tracks in the snow for the nature journal.

The cartwheel, step by step. First, a "bunny hop" over a line: hands down on one side, kick the feet over to the other side. Then, from a lunge with arms up, place one hand then the other along a line, legs going over, and land one foot then the other.

Colonial game: marbles. Draw a circle on the ground or tape one on the floor, and put marbles in the middle. Players take turns "shooting" a marble from outside the circle with a flick of the thumb, trying to knock marbles out. Keep the ones you knock out (or give them back at the end).
Indoor circuit; push-ups and curl-ups.
Snow play or a walk.
Jump-rope tricks: jumping on alternate feet (like running in place), and turning the rope backward.
The Virginia reel, complete. The head couple slides down the middle and back, then "reels" down the line, linking arms with each person in turn. Every couple takes a turn at the head.
Jog or jump rope 10 minutes.
A winter outing.
Skills checklist (below).
Dance the Virginia reel for the family, perhaps at Memory Work's Recitation Day this week.
Benchmark day: measure and record each benchmark on the sheet below. Compare with week 1.
A family winter walk.
Copy the week 1 numbers into the first column, so the child can see the change. Celebrate every improvement.

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: Jumps rope, one jump per turn
Does a safe forward roll, chin tucked
Holds two balances for five seconds
Does a cartwheel (or the bunny-hop stage)
Dances the Virginia reel with a partner

blocks.text: Safety in tumbling comes first: a soft surface, chin tucked, and one skill at a time. A cartwheel that stops at the bunny-hop stage is fine for this year.
Cold-day exercise counts in full. Indoor circuits and dancing are real PE.
The Virginia reel needs at least two couples; it's best with four or more. It's a lovely thing to dance at a co-op.
Virtue this term: Fortitude. Going out on a cold morning, or trying the cartwheel one more time, is fortitude in small things.

A jump rope for each child · a mat, folded blanket or soft carpet · tape for floor lines · hoops and beanbags for the obstacle course · marbles · fiddle music for the Virginia reel · warm layers, hats and gloves · water bottles

terms.title: Late Winter · Basketball Skills and Striking

head: Skills
Dribbling with the hands · chest and bounce passes · shooting · striking with a paddle · rolling a ball
rows: Dribble tag · keep-away · HORSE · paddle rally · four square · colonial game: nine-pins
Jog or jump rope 10 minutes · push-ups, curl-ups, sit-and-reach
A skill · B game · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Equipment note. A lowered hoop or a laundry basket on a chair works for shooting. A balloon makes a good first "ball" for paddle work.

blocks.text: Dribbling with the hands. Push the ball down with the fingertips, not the palm; keep it at waist height; look up, not at the ball. Dribble with one hand, then the other, standing still and then walking.
Dribble tag. Everyone dribbles a ball inside a small area; the tagger tries to tag others while dribbling. Lose your ball, and you're "it".
Jog or jump rope 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A walk.

Passing. Chest pass: hold the ball at the chest, step forward, push it straight to a partner's chest with both hands, thumbs ending down. Bounce pass: the same, but bounce it about two-thirds of the way to the partner.
Keep-away: two players pass while a third tries to intercept. Swap when the ball is caught.
Indoor or outdoor circuit; sit-and-reach.
A walk or bike ride.
Shooting. Remember B-E-E-F: Balance (feet apart), Eyes on the hoop, Elbow under the ball, Follow through, with the wrist flopping down "into the cookie jar". Shoot close to the hoop first.

HORSE. One player takes a shot; if it goes in, the next must make the same shot or earn a letter. Five letters (H-O-R-S-E) and you're out. Use a shorter word for younger siblings; or spell a Spelling word!
Jog 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A walk. Look for the first signs of spring for the nature journal.
Striking with a paddle. Start with a balloon: keep it in the air with a paddle (or a hand), watching it all the time. Then a soft ball, bounced once, hit with a flat paddle.
Paddle rally: two players hit a soft ball back and forth; count hits in a row.
Circuit; sit-and-reach.
A walk or outdoor play.
Rolling a ball underhand: step forward with the opposite foot, swing the arm back, and release the ball low and smooth.

Colonial game: nine-pins. Set up nine plastic bottles in a diamond. Roll a ball from a line and count the pins knocked down; two rolls each turn. Nine-pins was played in the colonies and is the ancestor of bowling. (Keeping score is Arithmetic practice.)
Jog 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A walk.
Skills checklist (below).

Four square. A square divided into four boxes, one player in each. Bounce the ball into another player's box; they hit it on after one bounce into another box. A miss sends that player to the lowest square.
Jog as long as you can, up to 10 minutes, and record it.
A family outing.

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: Dribbles with the fingertips, eyes up, with either hand
Makes a chest pass and a bounce pass to a partner
Shoots using balance, elbow and follow-through
Keeps a balloon or ball going with a paddle
Rolls a ball underhand toward a target

blocks.text: Lower the hoop. A child shooting at a ten-foot hoop learns bad habits. A basket on a chair, or a hoop at six or seven feet, is right for this age.
Four square is a classic playground game. Chalk the square on a driveway or tape it indoors.
Virtue this term: Justice. Fair play: following the rules, counting honestly, and giving everyone a turn, including the youngest.

A size 5 or junior basketball · a lowered hoop or a basket · balloons · a paddle (or a small racket) and a soft ball · nine plastic bottles and a ball for nine-pins · chalk or tape for four square · water bottles

terms.title: Spring · Softball Skills and Track and Field

head: Skills
Catching with a glove · batting from a tee · sprinting · the long jump · base running and throwing to a base
rows: Pickle · tee ball · relay races · a small softball game · a mini track meet · colonial game: graces
Jog 10 minutes · sprint practice · push-ups, curl-ups, sit-and-reach
A skill · B game · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Use soft balls. A soft "safety" softball or a tennis ball is right for this age, especially for catching.

blocks.text: Catching with a glove. For a ball above the waist, fingers of the glove up; below the waist, fingers down. For a ground ball, get low, glove on the ground, and close the other hand over it like an alligator's jaws.
Pickle. Two fielders with gloves stand at two bases; a runner tries to get from one base to the other without being tagged as the fielders throw back and forth.
Jog 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A spring hike.
Batting from a tee. Stand side-on to the tee, feet apart; hands together on the bat; elbows up; swing level and follow through; eyes on the ball.
Tee ball: a small game where every batter hits from the tee and runs. Everyone bats every inning.
Circuit; sit-and-reach.
A bike ride.
Sprinting. A ready position (one foot forward, knees bent), a quick start, and arms pumping hard from the shoulders. Run short sprints of 20–30 yards.
Relay races: teams take turns sprinting to a line and back, handing off a baton (a stick or a rolled paper).
Jog 10 minutes; sprints.
A longer hike.

The long jump. First the standing broad jump: swing the arms, jump forward off both feet, and land on both feet. Then a short run-up, take off from one foot, and land on two. Measure each jump with a tape measure. (Arithmetic: feet and inches.)

Colonial game: graces. Two players, each with two sticks and a ring (a small hoop or a ring of ribbon-wrapped card). Cross the sticks and pull them apart to toss the ring to a partner, who catches it on their sticks. Graces was a favorite game for colonial children.
Circuit; push-ups and curl-ups.
A walk or bike ride.
Base running and throwing to a base. Run through first base, don't slow down before it; round the base to go to second. Fielders throw overhand to the person covering a base.
A small softball game, using a soft ball, a tee or gentle underhand pitching, and short bases.
Jog 10 minutes; sit-and-reach.
A hike.

weeks.title: Review and a mini track meet

blocks.text: Skills checklist (below).
Mini track meet: a 50-yard sprint, a standing broad jump, a long jump with a run-up, and a relay. Record each child's results to beat next year.
Jog as long as you can, up to 10 minutes, and record it.
A family outing.

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: Catches with a glove, fingers up or down as needed
Hits a ball from a tee with a level swing
Sprints with a quick start and pumping arms
Does a standing broad jump, landing on two feet

blocks.text: Everyone bats, everyone plays. At this age there are no benches. Short innings, small teams, lots of turns.
Measure the jumps with the child doing the reading; it's real-world Arithmetic.
Virtue this term: Prudence. Thinking before acting in a game: looking before throwing, deciding whether to run for the next base or stay.
A child's glove · soft softballs or tennis balls · a bat and a batting tee · bases (or mats or cones) · a baton · a tape measure · sticks and rings for graces · water bottles and sunscreen

terms.title: Late Spring and Summer · Swimming, Field Day and the Year's Review

head: Skills
Water safety · floating · kicking and gliding · front crawl arms and breathing · swimming 25 yards (where available) · a frisbee and obstacle-course track for families without water
rows: Water games · frisbee keep-away · Field Day · family games
Swimming, hikes and long outdoor days
A skill · B game · C fitness · D outdoors (4 a week × 6 = 24)

glance.text: Two tracks this term. Track W (water) is for families with a pool, lake or swimming lessons. Track L (land) is for families without. Each week gives both; choose one.
Water safety is non-negotiable: an adult who can swim is always watching, within reach, and children never swim alone. A lifeguarded pool or lessons with an instructor are best.

blocks.text: W: Water safety and floating. Enter feet first; never swim alone; if someone is in trouble, reach (with a pole or towel) or throw (something that floats), don't go in. Then float on the back, ears in the water, tummy up, arms out like a star. L: Frisbee throw: grip with the thumb on top, step and flick the wrist so it spins flat.
W: Treasure dive: pick up rings from shallow water. L: Frisbee catch, counting catches in a row.
Jog 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A swim or a long walk.

W: Kicking and gliding. Hold the wall or a kickboard; flutter kick with straight legs from the hips, toes pointed. Then push off the wall and glide, face in the water, arms stretched forward. L: Frisbee catching: "pancake" catch, one hand above and one below.
W: Kickboard races in the shallow end. L: Frisbee keep-away: two players pass while a third tries to intercept.
Circuit; sit-and-reach.
A swim or a hike.

W: Front crawl arms and breathing. Arms reach forward one at a time and pull down under the body; turn the head to the side to breathe every two or three strokes. Practice standing in the shallow end first, then with a kickboard. L: Obstacle course skills: crawling, climbing, balancing and jumping over low objects.
W: Relay races across the shallow end. L: An outdoor obstacle course, timed.
Jog 10 minutes; push-ups and curl-ups.
A long outdoor day.
W: Swim 25 yards (or one length of a 25-yard pool) without stopping, using any stroke. Try it, rest, and try again. L: Review the year's skills: throwing, catching, kicking, dribbling, jumping rope.
Plan Field Day: the child helps choose the events and makes a list for week 35.
Circuit; sit-and-reach.
A swim or a hike.
Practice for Field Day.

Field Day, with family, friends or the co-op. Suggested events: a 50-yard sprint · a sack race · an egg-and-spoon race · a three-legged race · tug-of-war (Term 2) · hoop and stick (Term 1) · nine-pins (Term 4) · a water-balloon toss. Ribbons for everyone.
Light stretching after Field Day.
The whole day outdoors.
Skills checklist (below) for the term.
The child's favorite game of the whole year.
Benchmark day: measure and record each benchmark on the sheet below, and compare with weeks 1 and 18.
A celebration outing: a picnic, a swim, a hike.
Grade 3 goals (plan §4): a 10-minute jog, 20 rope jumps in a row, 10 catches in a row, and 25 yards of swimming where available. The others are personal bests: any improvement counts.

head: Skill
Confident
Not yet
rows: W: Knows the water-safety rules and can float on the back
W: Kicks and glides; swims 25 yards
L: Throws and catches a frisbee
Helped plan and took part in Field Day

head: Benchmarks
See the sheet above
rows: Yards: ___ · Water-safety rules known: yes / not yet
___ for the year (about 5,400 is the target: 150 × 36)

blocks.text: For Grade 4: Grades 3–5 continue the benchmarks; Grade 4 builds on these skills with more team play.
Swimming lessons are worth arranging if at all possible. Knowing how to swim is a safety skill for life.
Field Day is a celebration. Mix ages and abilities, and make sure every child wins something.
Keep moving over the summer. The year's games, swims and hikes don't need a manual.
Virtue this term: Charity. Cheering for others, helping a younger child in a race, and sharing equipment are charity on the playing field.

Swimsuits, towels, a kickboard and diving rings (Track W) · frisbees and obstacle-course items (Track L) · sacks, spoons and eggs (or potatoes), rope, balloons for Field Day · ribbons · sunscreen, hats and water bottles
